name: The Napoleon
line: A conqueror who strikes first and overturns the board
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Independent and Speed, this type believes that the actual strength of armies, more than diplomatic notes or treaties, decides outcomes, and trusts a result won by defeating the other side more than a peace bought with concessions. It acts on its own judgment rather than waiting for allies to agree, and, convinced that the other side grows stronger with time, it chooses to strike first. Measured against July 1914, it comes closest to the leader who hurries mobilization and sets short deadlines for ultimatums.

figure.name: Napoleon Bonaparte (Napoleon I)
figure.life: Born in 1769 in Ajaccio, Corsica, he studied at military schools in mainland France and became an artillery officer. He made his name at the siege of Toulon in 1793 and in the Italian campaign of 1796–1797, became First Consul after the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799, and took the title of emperor in 1804. In 1804 he issued the Napoleonic Code, which laid the foundations of modern civil law, but his successive wars of conquest left vast numbers of dead and wounded across Europe. After the failure of his Russian campaign in 1812 he abdicated in 1814 and went to Elba; he returned the following year, was defeated at Waterloo, and was exiled to St Helena in the South Atlantic, where he died in 1821.
figure.story: On 2 December 1805, near Austerlitz in Moravia (today Slavkov in the Czech Republic), Napoleon faced a combined Russian and Austrian army. He deliberately made his right wing look weak, drawing the allies down from the Pratzen Heights toward it, then seized the emptied center of the heights with Soult’s corps and cut the enemy army in two. After this victory Austria signed the Treaty of Pressburg on 26 December and left the war, and the Third Coalition collapsed.

kin.name: Hannibal Barca
kin.why: In 218 BC he led an army with war elephants across the Alps and struck first at the Roman heartland, and in 216 BC he encircled and crushed a Roman army at Cannae. His way of choosing the battlefield before the enemy was ready resembles Napoleon’s, and so does his failure, in the end, to force the enemy state to submit.

kin.name: Oda Nobunaga
kin.why: At Okehazama in 1560 he launched a surprise attack that shattered the far larger army of Imagawa Yoshimoto, changing the course of the Warring States period. He then pressed hard to unify Japan, but in 1582 he lost his life at the Honnō-ji temple in Kyoto when his retainer Akechi Mitsuhide rebelled.

you: Time and again you judged that you had to move before the other side finished its preparations. What you dislike most is missing a chance while waiting for someone else’s permission, and your aim is to secure a clear result in a short time. By the same token, you tend to shoulder the consequences of your decisions yourself rather than pass them on to others.
caution: It is easy to overlook that every victory adds to your enemies. After Austerlitz Napoleon kept widening the war, and in the Russian campaign of 1812 he lost most of his great army.

name: The Kutuzov
line: A patient guardian who yields ground but never surrenders
story: Giving up Moscow but refusing Napoleon a truce (1812)
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Independent and Caution, this type believes that strength decides the contest in the end and does not bow to the other side’s demands, but it never stakes all its strength on a single decisive battle. Rather than wait for help from others, it holds out with its own land and its own army, delaying the decision until time and distance wear the enemy down. It asks first what must be kept to the very end before counting what it loses today.

figure.name: Mikhail Kutuzov
figure.life: Born in St Petersburg in 1745 (some official records give 1747), he joined the army in his teens and gained experience fighting the Ottoman Empire under Suvorov. In 1774, in a battle near Alushta in Crimea, a bullet struck him in the temple and badly damaged his right eye, and in 1788 at the siege of Ochakov he was shot in the head again. At Austerlitz in 1805 he commanded the allied army, but Emperor Alexander I insisted on attacking over his objections and the allies suffered a heavy defeat; for some time afterward he was sidelined as a provincial governor. In May 1812 he concluded the Treaty of Bucharest with the Ottoman Empire, settling the southern front; in August that year he became commander-in-chief against Napoleon’s invasion, and in April of the following year he died at Bunzlau in Silesia while on campaign.
figure.story: After heavy losses at the battle of Borodino on 7 September 1812, Kutuzov decided at the council of Fili on 13 September to give up Moscow without a fight in order to save the army. On 5 October, at his camp at Tarutino, he received General Lauriston, whom Napoleon had sent from Moscow in hopes of peace, but he would not agree to a truce, saying only that he would pass the proposal on to the emperor, and so gained time. Alexander I refused to negotiate, and Napoleon, worn out by waiting, left Moscow on 19 October and began a brutal retreat.

kin.name: Trần Hưng Đạo (Trần Quốc Tuấn)
kin.why: When Mongol armies invaded in 1285 and in 1287–1288, he abandoned the capital, Thăng Long, and withdrew, leading a campaign to cut the invaders' supplies. In 1288 he had stakes driven into the bed of the Bạch Đằng estuary and destroyed the Mongol fleet on them at ebb tide.

kin.name: George Washington
kin.why: In the War of Independence he gave up New York and Philadelphia to the British but worked above all to keep the Continental Army intact, and on Christmas night 1776 he crossed the Delaware and surprised Trenton, reviving collapsing morale. Holding out while avoiding a great decisive battle, he received the British surrender at Yorktown in 1781 together with French forces, and in his Farewell Address of 1796 he advised the nation "to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world."

you: You have chosen not to kneel to the other side’s terms, even at a cost. You value the strength that will still be there at the end more than face or a single piece of ground today, and you are used to waiting until a hurried opponent wears himself out. You also know that this approach works only if you can endure the pressure and blame of those around you for a long time.
caution: It is easy to make light of the price paid while holding out. After Kutuzov gave up Moscow, most of the city burned in a great fire, and the wounded soldiers who could not be moved and the residents who stayed behind suffered terribly.

name: The Eisenhower
line: A commander who leads allied armies into the decisive battle
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Alliance and Speed, this type believes problems must be settled by force, but rather than fight alone it pools the armies and resources of its allies. It values the coordination that moves the generals and politicians of different nations under a single plan, and once preparations are complete it does not hesitate to seek the decisive battle. Among the leaders of 1914, it comes closest to one who aligns operations with allies and then moves swiftly to mobilize.

figure.name: Dwight D. Eisenhower
figure.life: Born in Denison, Texas, in 1890 and raised in Abilene, Kansas, he graduated from the US Military Academy at West Point in 1915. In the First World War he trained tank units in the United States and never reached the front, and for many years afterward he served as a staff officer. In the Second World War he commanded the landings in North Africa and then became Supreme Commander of the Allied Expeditionary Force; after the war he served as the first Supreme Allied Commander of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO). As president from 1953 to 1961 he concluded the armistice in the Korean War and warned against the military-industrial complex in his farewell address, but he was also criticized for approving covert operations that overthrew the governments of Iran and Guatemala.
figure.story: As the planned date for the landings approached in June 1944, a storm lashed the English Channel and Eisenhower postponed the operation by a day; when his meteorologists reported a brief break in the weather, he gave the final order to go in the early hours of 5 June. That same day he wrote out in advance a short statement in case the landings failed, taking the responsibility on himself: "If any blame or fault attaches to the attempt it is mine alone." On 6 June more than 150,000 troops, mainly American, British and Canadian, entered Normandy by sea and air.

kin.name: Scipio Africanus
kin.why: While Hannibal remained in Italy, he carried the fighting to Hispania and North Africa and joined forces with Masinissa of Numidia. At the battle of Zama in 202 BC, with Masinissa’s cavalry at his side, he defeated Hannibal and ended the Second Punic War.

kin.name: José de San Martín
kin.why: In 1817, together with Chile’s Bernardo O’Higgins, he led the Army of the Andes across the mountains and defeated the Spanish at Chacabuco. He then marched on Peru and declared its independence in 1821; the following year, after meeting Bolívar at Guayaquil, he gave up his command and withdrew.

you: You judged that winning together is surer than winning alone. You do not shirk the labor of aligning plans with allies, but once the preparations are done you do not put off the decision; you take the big step. And if things go badly, you are ready to take the responsibility yourself.
caution: The confidence that comes when allied armies move in one direction makes it easy to underrate the enemy’s capacity to strike back. Operation Market Garden, which Eisenhower approved in September 1944, failed, and that December the Germans took his armies by surprise in the Ardennes.

name: The Churchill
line: A lion who holds out to the end and waits for allies
traits: Leaning toward Power, Hardline, Alliance and Caution, this type believes force must be met with force when the other side pushes, and refuses a peace bought by compromising on bad terms. Yet it also knows it cannot win alone, so while it holds out it works hard to bring larger allies into the fight. Rather than rush to a decision, it thinks first about enduring for a long time without collapsing.

figure.name: Winston Churchill
figure.life: Born in 1874 at Blenheim Palace in Oxfordshire, the son of an aristocratic family, he traveled to Cuba, India, Sudan and South Africa as a cavalry officer and war correspondent, and made his name when he was captured in the Boer War and escaped. As First Lord of the Admiralty from 1911 he readied the fleet for war in 1914, but he left the post in 1915 after the failure of the Dardanelles operation, and in the 1930s he warned of the danger from Hitler yet was shunned in politics. He became prime minister on 10 May 1940 and led the country through the war; he lost the general election of 1945, became prime minister again in 1951, and received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1953. He is still criticized today for his imperialist views, including his opposition to the very end to self-government for India.
figure.story: When France surrendered in June 1940, Britain was left to face Germany alone in Europe; Churchill had already, at the end of May, rejected a proposal raised in the War Cabinet to sound out peace terms through Italy. In the Battle of Britain, fought from July to October, the Royal Air Force, relying on its radar early-warning network, held off the Luftwaffe’s offensive, and on 17 September Hitler postponed the invasion of Britain indefinitely. Throughout, Churchill kept asking Roosevelt for help, and the United States, by way of the Lend-Lease Act of March 1941, entered the war that December.

kin.name: Haile Selassie I
kin.why: When Italy invaded in 1935, he appealed for collective security before the League of Nations Assembly in Geneva the following year and held out in exile in Bath, England. He returned to Addis Ababa in 1941 after British forces and Ethiopian resistance fighters drove out the Italians, but in his last years, amid discontent over famine and stalled reform, he was deposed by the military in 1974.

kin.name: Yu Seong-ryong
kin.why: During the Imjin War against the Japanese invasions, he rose from Left State Councilor to Chief State Councilor and commissioner in charge of military affairs, directing the war effort: he led cooperation with the Ming relief army, the supply of grain to the troops and the reorganization of the military system, and kept the kingdom from collapse. Before the war he had recommended Yi Sun-sin for command, and after it he recorded his experience and his reflections in the Jingbirok (The Book of Corrections).

you: Even when the odds were against you, you chose to hold out rather than accept the other side’s terms. You admit that you cannot solve everything on your own strength, and aim instead to buy time until you can draw in nations that will fight beside you. Nor do you take lightly the power of words and symbols to keep up people’s morale.
caution: A refusal to back down easily turns into reckless operations. The attack on the Dardanelles that Churchill pushed as First Lord of the Admiralty in 1915, and the landings that followed it, cost enormous casualties and ended in withdrawal.

name: The Frederick
line: A gambler who seizes by surprise and keeps by negotiation
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Independent and Speed, this type moves first when the chance comes, takes what can be had, and is skilled at locking in the result through negotiation afterward. It trusts strength but does not cling to a fight to the finish, and it treats alliances as means to an end, ready to make a separate peace if need be. Its decisions are quick and its calculations clear, which also means it runs the risk of losing the trust of its neighbors.

figure.name: Frederick II (Frederick the Great)
figure.life: Born in Berlin in 1712, he clashed bitterly with his father, the stern soldier-king Frederick William I. In 1730 he was caught trying to flee abroad with his friend Hans Hermann von Katte and was made to watch Katte’s execution at the fortress of Küstrin. After taking the throne in 1740 he fought the Silesian Wars and the Seven Years' War and raised Prussia to the ranks of Europe’s great powers; he was also known as an enlightened monarch who played the flute and corresponded with Voltaire. In 1772 he divided Polish territory with Russia and Austria, and he died in 1786 at Sanssouci Palace in Potsdam.
figure.story: When Holy Roman Emperor Charles VI died in October 1740 and his daughter Maria Theresa inherited the Habsburg lands, Frederick marched into Austrian Silesia on 16 December that year without a declaration of war. After defeating the Austrians at Mollwitz in April 1741 he joined hands with France and others, but in June 1742 he made a separate preliminary peace with Austria at Breslau, gaining most of Silesia, and was the first to leave the war. Only after two more wars was the province confirmed as Prussian territory by the Treaty of Hubertusburg in 1763.

kin.name: Muhammad Ali
kin.why: As the Ottoman governor of Egypt, he sent his son Ibrahim to occupy Syria in 1831 and won recognition of his rule there in the Convention of Kütahya in 1833. Under pressure from the European powers in 1840 he gave up Syria, but through negotiation he kept the right to pass the governorship of Egypt to his descendants.

kin.name: James K. Polk
kin.why: In 1846 he settled the Oregon boundary with Britain at the 49th parallel by negotiation, and the same year he went to war with Mexico, gaining California, New Mexico and other vast lands in 1848. He was criticized by, among others, Abraham Lincoln, then a congressman, for provoking the war by sending troops into the disputed territory first.

you: You chose to move without hesitation when you saw an opening, but to leave the keeping of your gains to negotiation. You value the results actually left in your hands more than principle, and you think alliances and promises, too, can be recalculated for the sake of those results. Your judgment is quick and your sense of gain and loss is clear, but you need to factor in how others will remember you.
caution: Repeat a surprise that worked once, and your neighbors will readily combine against you. After striking Saxony first in 1756, Frederick found himself facing Austria, France and Russia at once, and in the Seven Years' War Prussia came close to collapse more than once.

name: The Tito
line: A pragmatist who walks the tightrope between great powers
story: Diplomacy outside both blocs after the break with Stalin (1948 on)
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Independent and Caution, this type holds that a country must have the strength to defend itself, yet rather than collide head-on with the great powers it sets them to check one another and draws practical gains from the space between them. It entrusts itself to neither camp, accepting help from both while letting neither push it around. It does not hurry, watching the other side’s moves and searching patiently for ways to cut its losses.

figure.name: Josip Broz Tito
figure.life: Born in 1892 in Kumrovec, in the Croatian lands of Austria-Hungary, he worked as a metalworker; in the First World War he fought in the Austro-Hungarian army, was wounded and became a prisoner of the Russians. He lived through the revolution in Russia, returned home a communist, spent years in prison, and from 1937 led the Communist Party of Yugoslavia. In the Second World War he led the Partisans against the German and Italian occupation, and after the war he governed the country for 35 years until his death in Ljubljana in 1980. He held together a federation of many nations and promoted his own brand of socialism based on workers' self-management, but under one-party rule he persecuted opponents, and after 1948 he confined people suspected of siding with the Soviet Union in the prison camp on the island of Goli Otok.
figure.story: On 28 June 1948 the Stalin-led Cominform expelled the Communist Party of Yugoslavia, but Tito did not yield to Soviet pressure and held to his own course. He went on to accept economic and military aid from the United States and the West without joining NATO, and in 1955, after Stalin’s death, Khrushchev came to Belgrade to mend relations. In 1961 he hosted the first summit of the Non-Aligned Movement in Belgrade, together with India’s Nehru, Egypt’s Nasser, Indonesia’s Sukarno and others.

kin.name: Menelik II
kin.why: He built up his army with weapons bought from Italy, France, Russia and elsewhere, and confronted Italy over the interpretation of the Treaty of Wuchale of 1889. After defeating the Italian army at the battle of Adwa in 1896, he won recognition of Ethiopia’s independence through negotiation, preserving his country while the European powers were carving up Africa.

kin.name: Chulalongkorn (Rama V)
kin.why: Caught between British Burma and Malaya and French Indochina, he gave up border territories on several occasions between 1893 and 1909 in exchange for keeping the core of the kingdom. Meanwhile he pushed through the abolition of slavery and administrative and military reforms, laying the groundwork for Siam to remain the only country in Southeast Asia never colonized by a European power.

you: Even facing a strong opponent, you did not hurry to take sides. You weigh what your country can actually gain and keep before causes or camps, and you aim for a position in which you are no one’s pawn yet obtain what you need from several sides. You know well that holding such a position takes constant calculation and patience.
caution: A balance that rests on one person’s skill is hard to sustain once that person is gone. A little more than a decade after Tito’s death, Yugoslavia broke apart amid ethnic conflict and went through war.

name: The Roosevelt
line: A pragmatist who builds alliances fast through deals
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Alliance and Speed, this type believes the balance of power decides outcomes, but rather than use force directly it prefers to build alliances quickly through deals. Unbound by form and procedure, it looks for terms that benefit both sides and proposes them first, and what it guards against most is losing a chance to a slow decision. It also works hard to win over public opinion by putting principle and interest forward together.

figure.name: Franklin D. Roosevelt
figure.life: Born in 1882 into a wealthy family in Hyde Park, New York, he graduated from Harvard and served as Assistant Secretary of the Navy during the First World War. In 1921, at 39, he was diagnosed with polio and lost the use of his legs, but he did not give up politics; he became governor of New York and then, in 1933, president. He fought the Great Depression with the New Deal, became the only president in American history to win four elections, and led the country through the Second World War until his death at Warm Springs, Georgia, on 12 April 1945. Executive Order 9066 of 1942, which opened the way to sending some 120,000 Japanese Americans to camps, is judged today to have been a grave wrong.
figure.story: In the summer of 1940 Britain was badly short of destroyers to fight German submarines, but the United States, officially neutral, could not easily hand over warships under its laws. Through an executive agreement that needed no ratification by Congress, Roosevelt agreed on 2 September to transfer 50 old destroyers in return for 99-year leases on bases in British territories in the Caribbean and elsewhere; Britain granted base rights in Newfoundland and Bermuda without payment. The deal led on to the Lend-Lease Act of the following March, opening the way for the United States to back Britain in practice even before it entered the war.

kin.name: Kim Chunchu (King Taejong Muyeol)
kin.why: When Silla lost the fortress of Daeya to a Baekje attack in 642, he went to Goguryeo to seek help, and the Nihon Shoki records that in 647 he crossed to Wa (Japan) and stayed for a time. In 648 he went to Tang China and concluded a military alliance with Emperor Taizong. After taking the throne in 654, he destroyed Baekje together with Tang forces in 660.

kin.name: Njinga Mbande
kin.country: Kingdoms of Ndongo and Matamba (present-day Angola)
kin.why: In 1621–1622 she went to Luanda as envoy of her brother the king to negotiate peace with Portugal, and was baptized there to seal the agreement. As queen she allied with the Dutch, who had taken Luanda in 1641, against Portugal, and in 1656 she made peace with Portugal and preserved her kingdom. Her deep involvement in the slave trade, including financing her wars with it, is also part of her record.

you: You were quick to reach out first rather than miss a chance. You value ways of getting things done over purity of principle, and you aim to find quickly where interests meet and build an alliance there. When procedure slows things down, you have no qualms about finding another way around it.
caution: Quick deals make it easy to trust the other side’s promises too far. The promise of free elections in Poland that Roosevelt obtained from Stalin at Yalta in February 1945 was never kept.

name: The Bismarck
line: An alliance architect who designs the balance of power
traits: Leaning toward Power, Bargain, Alliance and Caution, this type sees power as the foundation of international relations, but uses it to weave a balance among many states rather than to wage war. It believes it can deal even with potential enemies, and it layers alliance upon alliance so that no single state can overturn the order on its own. Its aim is to avoid a great war, and it moves carefully, one step at a time.

figure.name: Otto von Bismarck
figure.life: Born in 1815 into a Junker (landed noble) family at Schönhausen, east of the Elbe, he served as a diplomat at the Federal Diet in Frankfurt, in St Petersburg and in Paris. Becoming minister-president of Prussia in 1862, he pushed through military expansion with his "blood and iron" speech, and after wars with Denmark in 1864, Austria in 1866 and France in 1870–1871 he founded the German Empire in 1871. As imperial chancellor he repressed the Catholic Church and the socialists, yet introduced the world’s first national social insurance system, and after unification he sought to keep the peace of Europe through alliance diplomacy rather than war. He was forced out in 1890 after clashing with the young Emperor Wilhelm II, and died in 1898 at Friedrichsruh near Hamburg.
figure.story: In 1887, when the League of the Three Emperors came to an end because Russia and Austria were at odds over Bulgaria, Bismarck secretly concluded the Reinsurance Treaty with Russia on 18 June. If either country went to war with a third power, the other would stay neutral, except where Germany attacked France or Russia attacked Austria. It was a device to keep the alliance with Austria while preventing Russia and France from joining hands, but in 1890, the year Bismarck left office, Germany did not renew it.

kin.name: Li Hongzhang
kin.why: As Commissioner of the Northern Ports (Beiyang) he ran Qing diplomacy, trying to play the powers off against one another on the principle of "using barbarians to control barbarians"; in 1882 he arranged for Joseon Korea to sign a treaty with the United States as a check on Japan and Russia. After the Sino-Japanese War, in 1896, he concluded a secret alliance with Russia, but he could not halt the decline of the Qing.

kin.name: Moshoeshoe I
kin.why: He took in groups fleeing the wars of the region and built the Basotho nation around the mountain stronghold of Thaba Bosiu, conducting diplomacy among the Boers, the British and the missionaries. As wars with the Orange Free State cost him land, he accepted British protection in 1868, laying the basis for Lesotho’s survival as an independent country today.

you: You cared more about building a structure in which the other side would not come at you again than about defeating it. You do not fix friends and enemies in place but adjust relations as needed, aiming for an order in which your country’s position endures without a great war. You tend to picture the situation a few years ahead before thinking of the victory in front of you.
caution: A web of alliances that only its designer can manage tends to unravel once he leaves. After Bismarck’s departure the Reinsurance Treaty lapsed, Russia allied with France in 1894, and that line of confrontation held until 1914.

name: The de Gaulle
line: A man of principle who raises the flag alone
story: The Appeal of 18 June from London (1940)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Independent and Speed, this type believes that legitimacy and principle, more than force, win in the end, and it accepts no compromise that violates principle. It does not wait for others to decide; it states its position clearly and first, alone if necessary, and rallies people to it. It insists on equal standing even with allies, putting its country’s prestige first even when it is the one receiving help.

figure.name: Charles de Gaulle
figure.life: Born in Lille in 1890, he graduated from the Saint-Cyr military academy; in the First World War he was wounded and captured at Verdun in 1916 and made several attempts to escape. In the 1930s he argued for mobile warfare built around armored forces, without success, and when the German army overran France in June 1940 he went to London and led Free France. After the liberation of Paris in 1944 he headed the provisional government; returning to power in 1958 amid the Algerian crisis, he founded the Fifth Republic and in 1962 accepted Algerian independence. As president he built an independent nuclear force and in 1966 withdrew France from NATO’s integrated military command; after losing a referendum in 1969 he stepped down, and he died the following year at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises.
figure.story: When Pétain announced on 17 June 1940 that he would seek an armistice, de Gaulle, then under-secretary for national defense, crossed to London, and the next day, 18 June, he called for resistance on BBC radio, declaring that the war would not end with the defeat in France: "This war is a world war." At the time he was a temporary brigadier general whose name was almost unknown, and in August that year a Vichy military court sentenced him to death in absentia. Even so, the Free France he founded gradually rallied overseas colonies and resistance forces at home, and in August 1944 it entered Paris alongside the Allies.

kin.name: Simón Bolívar
kin.why: Even when repeated defeats early in the wars of independence drove him into exile in Jamaica in 1815, he did not give up, setting out the case for the independence of Spanish America in a letter. With help from Haiti he returned to the fight, and after the victory at Boyacá in 1819 he led the way to independence for present-day Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, Bolivia and other countries.

kin.name: Kim Ku
kin.country: Korea (Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea)
kin.why: He kept the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea alive to the end as it moved from Shanghai all the way to Chongqing, and in 1932 he led the Korean Patriotic Organization in planning the attacks carried out by Yi Bong-chang and Yun Bong-gil. After liberation he tried to prevent the division of the country, taking part in the North–South talks of 1948, and on 26 June of the following year he was shot dead by An Du-hui at Gyeonggyojang, his residence in Seoul.

you: Even when the odds were against you, you chose to put principle first and proclaim it openly, alone if need be. You consider it more important to make clear the legitimacy your country must uphold than to shift position to suit other nations' calculations. Even when receiving help you want to be treated as an equal, and you accept that this will often bring you into conflict with your partners.
caution: Stubbornness in defense of prestige easily spills over into friction with partners. During the war de Gaulle and Roosevelt traded deep mistrust, and de Gaulle was not even invited to the Yalta Conference of 1945.

name: The Gandhi
line: A resister who holds to nonviolence to the end
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Independent and Caution, this type refuses to overpower the other side by force and makes fidelity to a principle it believes right its strongest instrument. It will not yield an inch on principle, but instead of violence or surprise it chooses pressure and persuasion sustained over a long time. Rather than borrow others' strength, it sets an example itself so that people follow.

figure.name: Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi
figure.life: Born in Porbandar in western India in 1869, he studied law in London and from 1893 spent about twenty years in South Africa resisting discrimination against Indians, refining satyagraha, a method of nonviolent resistance. Returning to India in 1915, he led the Indian National Congress in the Non-Cooperation Movement, the Salt March and the Quit India movement, and was imprisoned many times. On caste he clashed sharply with Ambedkar, a leader born into an "untouchable" community, and remarks he made about Africans during his South African years draw criticism today. India won independence in 1947, but partition from Pakistan brought mass violence, and while appealing for reconciliation between religions Gandhi was shot dead in New Delhi on 30 January 1948 by the Hindu nationalist Nathuram Godse.
figure.story: On 12 March 1930, defying Britain’s salt monopoly law, Gandhi set out from the Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad with 78 companions, walked some 390 km, and on the morning of 6 April, on the beach at Dandi on the Arabian Sea, picked up a lump of salty mud, breaking the salt law. As news of the march spread, huge numbers of people across India broke the salt laws and tens of thousands were arrested; Gandhi himself was arrested in May. The campaign led to the Gandhi–Irwin Pact the following year and to his attendance at the Round Table Conference in London.

kin.name: Martin Luther King Jr.
kin.why: Beginning with the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955–1956, he fought the system of racial segregation through nonviolent civil disobedience, and at the March on Washington in 1963 he gave his "I Have a Dream" speech. He studied Gandhi’s thought deeply, and he was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

kin.name: Václav Havel
kin.why: A playwright who called for "living in truth" under the communist regime, he was a driving force behind the human rights declaration Charter 77 in 1977 and afterward spent years in prison for his dissident activity. In 1989 he led the Velvet Revolution, which changed the regime without violence, and became president.

you: You cared as much about how you win as about winning. Even when an easy shortcut was there, you did not take it if it went against principle, choosing instead, however long it took, the path by which the other side loses its own legitimacy. What you aim for is not a result won by force but one that people accept as right.
caution: A decision to keep faith with principle can bewilder those who stand with you. In February 1922, after a crowd set fire to a police station in a village in northern India and 22 policemen died, Gandhi abruptly halted the nationwide Non-Cooperation Movement, provoking a strong backlash even within the Congress.

name: The Truman
line: An enforcer who steps in the moment the rules are broken
story: The decision to enter the Korean War (1950)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Alliance and Speed, this type holds that a breach of the rules of international order must not be left to stand, and it responds with action, not words alone. Rather than step forward alone, it acts in the name of international organizations or allies to give its response legitimacy. It does not drag out decisions, and it makes plain that it will carry their weight itself.

figure.name: Harry S. Truman
figure.life: Born in Lamar, Missouri, in 1884, he never finished college and worked at farming and many other jobs; in the First World War he fought in France as an artillery captain. When the men’s clothing store he opened after the war went under, he entered local politics and rose to the Senate, and in 1945, less than three months after becoming vice president, he succeeded to the presidency on Roosevelt’s death. In August 1945 he approved the atomic bombing of Japan, a decision that some still credit with ending the war sooner and others condemn for killing civilians on a massive scale. With the Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin Airlift and the founding of NATO he set the course of US foreign policy in the early Cold War, and in 1948 he issued an executive order ending racial segregation in the armed forces.
figure.story: When North Korean forces crossed the 38th parallel and invaded the South on 25 June 1950, the Truman administration immediately took the matter to the UN Security Council, securing a resolution that same day demanding the withdrawal of North Korean forces and, on 27 June, a resolution recommending that member states assist South Korea. The Soviet Union, boycotting the Council over the question of China’s representation, could not use its veto. Truman approved US naval and air support on 27 June and the commitment of ground forces on 30 June, and in July a United Nations Command was formed under MacArthur.

kin.name: William III of Orange (William III of England)
kin.why: When Louis XIV’s France invaded the Netherlands in 1672 and the country was in peril, he became stadtholder and led the resistance, and for the rest of his life he assembled coalitions of states against Louis XIV’s expansion. In 1688 he landed swiftly in England and carried out the Glorious Revolution, and the following year he accepted Parliament’s Bill of Rights.

kin.name: Julius Nyerere
kin.why: When Idi Amin’s Uganda invaded the Kagera region of northwestern Tanzania in 1978 and declared it annexed, he struck back at once. Advancing together with Ugandan exile forces, the Tanzanian army took the capital, Kampala, in April 1979, and Amin fled the country.

you: You saw that leaving a rule-breaker alone invites something worse next time, and you chose to respond without hesitation. But you want that response to be one that many nations endorse together, not force wielded alone. At your core is a refusal to push hard decisions onto others and a readiness to take them on yourself.
caution: When a quick response succeeds, it is tempting to widen the goal. After the Truman administration approved the advance north of the 38th parallel in the fall of 1950, China entered the war, and the fighting went on until the armistice of July 1953.

name: The Mandela
line: A reconciler who stands firm, waits, and wins through negotiation
story: Ending apartheid through negotiation after 27 years in prison (1990–1994)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Hardline, Alliance and Caution, this type does not bend on justice and principle, yet its goal is not to destroy the other side but to make both live together under the same rules. It builds pressure by widening its base of support at home and abroad, and it knows how to wait a long time, until the other side has no choice but to negotiate. Even after winning, it chooses reconciliation over revenge to steady the new order.

figure.name: Nelson Mandela
figure.life: Born in 1918 into the royal house of the Thembu at Mvezo in eastern South Africa, he became a lawyer and in 1952 opened, with Oliver Tambo, South Africa’s first Black law firm. In the African National Congress (ANC) he fought apartheid, the system of racial segregation, and when the nonviolent movement was crushed by force, he led the founding of the armed organization Umkhonto we Sizwe in 1961. Arrested in 1962, he was sentenced to life imprisonment at the Rivonia Trial in 1964 and spent more than 27 years behind bars, on Robben Island and elsewhere. Released in 1990, he led the negotiations, shared the Nobel Peace Prize with de Klerk in 1993, became president after the first democratic election in 1994, and stepped down after a single term.
figure.story: In 1985, when President Botha offered to free him if he renounced violence, Mandela refused a conditional release, answering that "only free men can negotiate." From the end of that year he began secret contacts with government figures from inside prison, and after his release on 11 February 1990 he kept the negotiations going through waves of political violence, bringing about in April 1994 the first election in which all races took part. As president he set up the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, putting the uncovering of truth and reconciliation ahead of punishment.

kin.name: Abraham Lincoln
kin.why: He never accepted the secession of the South, yet he chose his moments with care, waiting for the victory at Antietam in 1862 to issue the Emancipation Proclamation. In his second inaugural address in 1865 he called on the nation to act "with malice toward none, with charity for all" and "to bind up the nation’s wounds," but he was assassinated that April.

kin.name: Konrad Adenauer
kin.why: Mayor of Cologne until the Nazis drove him out in 1933, he became West Germany’s first chancellor in 1949 at the age of 73. While steadily strengthening the alliance with the West, he reconciled with the old enemy France and in 1963 signed the Élysée Treaty with de Gaulle.

you: You did not retreat on principle, yet you chose to draw the other side onto a path of living together rather than to break it. You are not impatient even when gathering supporters and building pressure takes a long time, and you think first about what order will remain after you win. For you, victory is closer to winning the other side’s consent than its surrender.
caution: Putting reconciliation first can fall out of step with the pace of change your supporters want. Mandela’s government achieved political peace but was criticized for not greatly narrowing the economic inequality between Black and white South Africans.

name: The Sadat
line: A negotiator who walks into the heart of the enemy camp
story: The visit to Jerusalem and the Camp David Accords (1977–1978)
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Independent and Speed, this type makes international law and legitimacy the basis of negotiation and believes that even a long-blocked situation can be unlocked by a deal. Rather than wait for the consent of allies or neighbors, it goes in person, alone if need be, into the other camp to settle matters face to face. When a chance to change the situation appears, it moves fast and accepts the risk.

figure.name: Anwar Sadat
figure.life: Born in 1918 in the village of Mit Abu al-Kum in the Nile Delta, he graduated from the military academy in 1938 and was jailed twice, during and after the Second World War, for opposing British rule. He took part in the Free Officers' revolution led by Nasser in 1952 and became president on Nasser’s death in 1970. After expelling Soviet military advisers in 1972, he launched a surprise attack on Israel together with Syria in October 1973 and crossed the Suez Canal, then used the bargaining power won in that war to move closer to the United States. In September 1981 he had some 1,500 critics arrested in a single sweep, and a month later, on 6 October, he was assassinated by Islamist officers at a victory parade.
figure.story: On 9 November 1977, in a speech to the Egyptian parliament, Sadat said that for the sake of peace he would go even to the Israeli parliament, and on 19 November he actually arrived in Jerusalem, addressing the Knesset the next day. It was the first official visit to Israel by the head of an Arab state. The following September, with US President Carter mediating, he concluded the Camp David Accords with Israeli Prime Minister Begin, and in March 1979 he signed a peace treaty that opened the way to recovering the Sinai Peninsula.

kin.name: Seo Hui
kin.why: When the Khitan commander Xiao Sunning invaded with a large army in 993, he went into the enemy camp to negotiate. Arguing that Goryeo was the successor of Goguryeo, and offering to establish relations with the Khitan once the Jurchen of the Yalu River basin were driven out, he persuaded the army to withdraw, and Goryeo then gained the six garrison districts east of the river.

kin.name: Willy Brandt
kin.why: After becoming chancellor in 1969 he pursued Ostpolitik, meeting the East German premier for the first time at Erfurt in 1970 and signing treaties with the Soviet Union and Poland. That December he knelt before the memorial to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising in atonement for the crimes of Nazi Germany, and he received the Nobel Peace Prize the following year.

you: You were convinced that a long-blocked problem is solved only when someone moves first, and you chose to take that first step yourself. Ready for opposition and misunderstanding around you, you aim to sit down directly with the other side and produce a result. Holding principle and bargaining together, you go into a negotiation with a clear line between what you can concede and what you must keep.
caution: Get too far ahead alone and your allies and supporters at home may not follow. Sadat’s separate peace with Israel led to the suspension of Egypt’s membership in the Arab League, and in the end he died at the hands of opponents at home.

name: The Talleyrand
line: A diplomat of survival who makes principle his weapon
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Independent and Caution, this type believes that even from a position of weakness it can win a seat at the table by invoking principles and rules. Bound to no camp, it changes partners as circumstances require, and it waits without hurry for cracks to open among its rivals. A realist, it does not shrink from abandoning yesterday’s position if that is what it takes to protect the result.

figure.name: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord
figure.life: Born in Paris in 1754 to an old noble family, he had a lame leg and so entered the church instead of the army, becoming bishop of Autun in 1788. Early in the French Revolution he proposed nationalizing church property, and when the revolution turned radical he lived in exile in Britain and the United States. He served as foreign minister under the Directory and under Napoleon, but after leaving office in 1807 he turned against Napoleon; in 1814 he engineered the Bourbon Restoration, and in the 1830s, as ambassador in London, he handled the question of Belgian independence. Having survived revolution, empire and monarchy alike, he was dogged all his life by charges of opportunism and of taking bribes, and he died in Paris in 1838.
figure.story: When the Congress of Vienna opened in September 1814, France was a defeated power, but Talleyrand, invoking the principle of "legitimacy," the restoration of the rightful dynasties and order of the time before the Revolution, won France a place in the great powers' deliberations. When Russia and Prussia faced off against Austria and Britain over Saxony and Poland, he concluded a secret defensive treaty with Austria and Britain on 3 January 1815, restoring France as one of the pillars of the great-power system. Napoleon’s Hundred Days made the peace terms far heavier, but at the Congress of Aix-la-Chapelle (Aachen) in 1818 France was readmitted to the ranks of the great powers.

kin.name: Wellington Koo (Gu Weijun)
kin.why: At the Paris Peace Conference of 1919, when Germany’s rights in Shandong were handed to Japan, he, as a member of the Chinese delegation, invoked international law and the principle of national self-determination and led the refusal to sign the Treaty of Versailles. At the Washington Conference of 1922 he helped secure the agreement that returned Shandong to China.

kin.name: Baron of Rio Branco (José Maria da Silva Paranhos Júnior)
kin.why: Representing Brazil in international arbitrations of its boundary disputes with Argentina in 1895 and with French Guiana in 1900, he proved his country’s rights with old maps and treaty documents and won both cases. As foreign minister from 1902 until his death, he settled most of Brazil’s borders through negotiation and arbitration, without war.

you: When strength was lacking, you chose to win a place at the table by invoking rules and legitimacy. Rather than stay long on one side, you watch how things develop and pick the path of least loss, aiming above all for your country’s survival. Changing position along the way does not trouble you much.
caution: Change sides often and you may keep the result but lose trust. Despite his great success at Vienna, Talleyrand never shook off the distrust owed to a man who had abandoned revolution, empire and monarchy in turn, and after resigning as prime minister in September 1815 in protest at the harsh terms of the Second Treaty of Paris, he spent fifteen years on the margins of power.

name: The Kennedy
line: A negotiator who builds a way out of a crisis
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Alliance and Speed, this type judges quickly when crisis strikes, but seeks a way out within the framework of rules rather than through armed clash. It secures the support of allies and international organizations to strengthen the legitimacy of its pressure, while preparing a deal that lets the other side back down without losing face. It tries to apply hard pressure and keep the door to negotiation open at the same time.

figure.name: John F. Kennedy
figure.life: Born in 1917 into a wealthy Irish American family in Brookline, Massachusetts, he graduated from Harvard and in the Second World War commanded the torpedo boat PT-109 in the Pacific. After serving in the House and the Senate, in January 1961, at 43, he became the youngest person ever elected president of the United States. In April 1961, three months after he took office, the Bay of Pigs invasion spearheaded by Cuban exiles failed, and he is also judged to have paved the way for the later escalation of the war in Vietnam by greatly increasing the number of military advisers sent there. In June 1963 he gave a speech calling for peace with the Soviet Union, and in August he concluded the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty, but on 22 November that year he was assassinated in Dallas.
figure.story: On 16 October 1962 Kennedy was shown reconnaissance photographs revealing that the Soviet Union was building bases for medium-range nuclear missiles in Cuba. Instead of the air strike his military chiefs urged, he announced a naval "quarantine" on 22 October and won the backing of the Organization of American States as grounds for the blockade. On 27 October, through his brother Robert Kennedy, he conveyed to the Soviets a pledge not to invade Cuba together with a willingness to remove the Jupiter missiles from Turkey in secret, and the next day Khrushchev announced that the missiles in Cuba would be withdrawn.

kin.name: Dag Hammarskjöld
kin.why: In January 1955 he traveled to Beijing, capital of the People’s Republic of China, which had no diplomatic relations with the United States, and negotiated directly with Zhou Enlai, opening the way for the release that year of all 15 American airmen captured during the Korean War. In 1961 he was killed in a plane crash while on his way to mediate a ceasefire in the Congo conflict; the cause of the crash has never been clearly established.

kin.name: Lester Pearson
kin.why: During the Suez Crisis of 1956, as Canada’s foreign minister, he proposed the creation of the UN Emergency Force, giving British, French and Israeli forces a way to withdraw from Egypt without great loss of face. For this he received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1957, and he later became prime minister of Canada.

you: When crisis struck, you chose to look for a path that neither retreats nor charges in blindly. You aim to raise the pressure while also holding out an exit the other side can accept, and along the way you treat the support of allies as a precious asset. You are used to hearing many views in a short time and then making the call.
caution: Quick decisions easily lead to the mistake of adopting inherited plans without enough scrutiny. Shortly after taking office, Kennedy approved the Bay of Pigs invasion plan prepared under the previous administration, and it collapsed within three days.

name: The Metternich
line: A designer who keeps order through conferences
traits: Leaning toward Rules, Bargain, Alliance and Caution, this type believes order can be kept through conferences and treaties rather than war, and works hard to create rules that many states uphold together. It finds compromises among states with differing interests and values predictable stability above sudden change. Without hurrying, it designs frameworks meant to last.

figure.name: Klemens von Metternich
figure.life: Born in 1773 in Koblenz on the Rhine, the son of a noble family, he moved with his family to Vienna when French revolutionary armies occupied the Rhineland. After serving as ambassador in Dresden, Berlin and Paris he became foreign minister in 1809, and in 1810 he arranged the marriage of Napoleon to the Austrian archduchess Marie Louise, buying his country breathing space. After joining the coalition against France in 1813 he presided over the Congress of Vienna, and for more than thirty years afterward he was the central figure of Europe’s conservative order. Through the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819 he imposed censorship on the press and the universities and suppressed liberal and nationalist movements; driven from office by the revolution of March 1848, he took refuge in England, and he died in Vienna in 1859.
figure.story: At the Congress of Vienna, held from September 1814 to June 1815 after Napoleon’s defeat, Metternich as its president reconciled the interests of the great powers and built a balance in which no single state could dominate Europe. The powers then met again and again, at Aix-la-Chapelle in 1818, Troppau in 1820, Laibach in 1821 and Verona in 1822, to handle disputes through consultation, a system known as the "Concert of Europe." Under it there was no major war among the European great powers until the Crimean War broke out in 1853.

kin.name: Jean Monnet
kin.why: A cognac merchant by background, he coordinated Allied supply in both world wars, drafted the Schuman Declaration in 1950, and became the first president of the High Authority of the European Coal and Steel Community. He never stood for election, but for his work to remove the causes of war through conferences and institutions he is called the "father of European integration."

kin.name: Léopold Sédar Senghor
kin.why: A poet and a leading thinker of the Négritude movement, he served as president for twenty years after Senegal’s independence in 1960, emphasizing cooperation with France and consultation among African states. In 1980 he resigned of his own accord before his term was over, setting a precedent for the peaceful transfer of power in Africa.

you: You valued rules that endure over a single victory. You do not find it tiresome to bring states with differing interests together to find common ground, and you aim for predictable stability over sudden change. Your calculation is to secure, within that order, a respected place for your country.
caution: In guarding stability it is easy to suppress the voices that want change. The order Metternich defended for some thirty years was shaken by revolutions across Europe in 1848, and he himself was driven out of Vienna.
